newsitem.title: FRANCE: France cuts stake in computer maker Bull.
newsitem.headline: France cuts stake in computer maker Bull.

text.p: The French government will soon sell 19 million shares in computer maker Bull, cutting its stake to about 17 percent and allowing private investors to buy shares, the company said on Thursday.

The government has 30.5 percent in Cie des Machines Bull since the latest stake reduction, on February 25, when the state sold large tranches to industrial investors which put the former state-owned high-technology group mainly in private hands.
After the sale it will have a stake in Bull equal to those of France Telecom , NEC Corp of Japan and Motorola Inc of the United States.
IBM has 0.7 percent, company staff 3.5 percent and 3.4 percent is currently on the market.

The price of the sale will be announced by the Finance Ministry after advise by the independent Privatisation Commission. At its current market price of 52 francs per share, the state would be able to raise 1.04 billion francs.

Bull said it would have between 15 and 20 percent of its shares on the market and would ask for its shares to be listed on the main monthly settlement market of the Paris Bourse, instead its current cash market listing.
Bull is also listed in Germany and Switzerland.
Bull said that the share sale, to private people and institutional investors, would be realised in the "shortest possible time."
At the Finance Ministry there was no immediate comment on the timing.
Bull said that the sale would allow the Bull shares to become "one of the few European high technology shares."
It added that the Bull staff would be able to buy up to 10 percent of the company's share capital.
Bull re-affirmed its forecast of a significant increase in its 1997 net income.
Bull's 1996 net profit increased by 23 percent to 376 million francs ($66.3 million). It had returned to the black in 1995 after running up losses of 22 billion francs since 1989.
Early last year, Bull merged its U.S. Zenith Data Systems personal computer (PC) unit with Packard Bell Electronics Inc to form, at least on paper, the world's biggest PC maker.

Bull chairman Jean-Marie Descarpentries, brought in by the state in 1993 to turn round the company and make it ready for privatisation, has for a time been looking for a fourth big, European, industrial partner to take a 17 percent stake, but the search was long and fruitless due to the difficulties of other European computer groups such as Olivetti of Italy.
